name: Wayu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Michailovsky, Boyd (1988) La langue hayu. Paris: Éditions du CNRS.
earlier_scan.note: Michailovsky 2017 Hayu chapter (HAL halshs-01486506) WAS loaded: phonology covers length/nasality but states nothing on stress; the 1988 full grammar plausibly does and is print-only.

sources.citation: WALS Online, language Hayu (wals code hay; sources Michailovsky 1981, 1988, 2003); WALS CLDF cldf-datasets/wals, master).
sources.access_detail: read online, no copy kept
sources.note: 46 WALS values coded for Hayu, none for the stress chapters 14A-17A (Goedemans & van der Hulst); Hayu is not in StressTyp2's language list either (StressTyp2.ullet.net checked).

sources.citation: Hodgson, Brian H. 1874. Essays on the Languages, Literature, and Religion of Nepál and Tibet. London: Trübner.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Does not contain the Vayu grammar (refers the reader to JASB); its accent remarks concern the 'Tartar'/Gyarung vocabularies, not Vayu.

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd. 2017. Hayu. In Thurgood & LaPolla (eds), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 2nd ed., 680-695. London: Routledge. (author preprint; same text as the 2003 1st-edition chapter pp. 518-532)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §2 Phonology (syllable canon, seven vowels, length distinctive in open first syllables of polysyllabic words, nasality, consonants): no statement on stress, accent or tone (confirms the earlier scan note).

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd. 1974. Hayu typology and verbal morphology. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 1(1): 1-26.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Appendix 'Phonology and Transcription' (pp. 18-20) covers length (distinctive only in open initial syllables) and final-consonant allophony; refers to Kailash 1973 for the phonology. No mention of stress, accent or tone.

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd. 2017. Kiranti languages. In Thurgood & LaPolla (eds), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge. (author preprint)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §2.5 'Tone, Stress' (p. 7 of preprint): tone in Sunwar/Thulung/Khaling; 'Predictable, fixed stress has been described in several languages (e.g. Belhare, Dumi (van Driem 1993), Wambule); a stress opposition is reported on polysyllabic words in Sangpang (Huysmans 2007).' Hayu is not mentioned under stress.

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd. 1988. Phonological typology of Nepal languages. LTBA 11(2): 25-50.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Areal survey of 20 Nepal languages incl. Hayu (Murajor). Tone/register map places Hayu among the non-tonal languages; length map notes Hayu long vowels restricted to initial syllable. Stress/accent is not among the surveyed features; no stress statement for Hayu.

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd. 1975. A case of rhinoglottophilia in Hayu. LTBA 2(2): 293.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: One page on glottalized final stops before /h/; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Mazaudon, Martine. 1974. Notes on tone in Tibeto-Burman. LTBA 1(1): 27-54.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: General discussion of tone and stress in Tibeto-Burman; Hayu is not mentioned.

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd & Martine Mazaudon. 1973. Notes on the Hayu language. Kailash 1(2): 135-152 (Part 1: Hayu phonology).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Full phonology of the Murajor dialect. §1.13 'Tone' (pp. 139-140): tone re-investigated for two weeks; 'No distinctive or even consistent non-intonational pitch or melodic patterns were found.' §1.22 (p. 141): vowel length distinctive only in open initial syllables of polysyllabic words. No mention of stress or accent anywhere.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.), Sten Konow. 1909. Linguistic Survey of India vol. III, part 1 (Tibeto-Burman family: Tibetan and Himalayan dialects), Vayu section pp. 382ff.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Pronunciation' paragraph (p. 382), entirely based on Hodgson: repeats the abrupt tone (slurred final consonants) and pausing tone; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Hodgson, Brian H. 1880 [1857-58]. Grammatical analysis of the Vayu language: A. Vayu vocabulary, B. Vayu grammar. In Miscellaneous Essays relating to Indian Subjects, vol. 1, 216-319. London: Trübner (reprint of JASB 26-27).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology section. Footnotes note an 'abrupt tone/accent' (glottalized/dropped final consonant) and a 'pausing tone' (vowel prolongation) in verb forms and demonstratives (p. 272 fn., p. 301 fn.: 'There is not only no abrupt accent or tone, but there is an equally forcible pausing tone'). These are segmental/length phenomena, not word stress; nothing on stress placement.
